transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-09-14 15:04 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-09-14T15:04:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 26.45 degrees and its azimuth is 208.31 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 7.011 degrees and its azimuth is 167.666 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 13.37 percent illuminated, 42.804 degrees from the Sun, and 391679.7 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not reliably with the unaided eye, despite it being geometrically above the horizon.

The Moon is only about 13% illuminated—a thin crescent—and is just 7° above the horizon. In bright daylight, the low altitude is especially unfavorable: atmospheric extinction, haze near the horizon, and reduced contrast will make the crescent much fainter and harder to distinguish. Its 42.8° separation from the Sun is reasonably safe and gives you a useful direction, but it is not enough to overcome the bright sky and low elevation in typical conditions.

With exceptionally transparent air and a very careful search, you might catch it—look roughly south-southeast (azimuth 168°), about a fist-width above the horizon, preferably using a distant building, hill, or other reference to fix the altitude. But for an ordinary observer, “clear sky” alone does not make it likely.

Do not use binoculars or a telescope to sweep the sky anywhere near the Sun.
